svg.aria-label: The back of a standing torso with the seven spinal landmarks a student can find by hand, and with the published error rate attached to each one that has one: C7 is the most prominent spinous in only about 60 to 70 percent of people, the supracristal plane crosses L5 rather than L4 in about 20 percent, and the T7 correspondence holds only with the arms at the sides.

g.text: Palpable landmarks, from behind
standing, with the arms hanging at the sides
scapula
iliac crest

g.data-tip: The bony ridge in the midline at the base of the skull. Run a finger up the back of the neck until it stops. Every level you count off below the skull starts from here.
g.text: External occipital protuberance
the ridge at the base of the skull

g.data-tip: The first spinous process you can feel below the skull, because the arch of C1 carries no spinous process to find. It is a fixed starting point in a way that C7 is not.
g.text: C2 spinous process
the first bone you can feel below the skull

g.data-tip: Easiest to find with the neck bent forward. But C7 is the most prominent spinous process in only about 60 to 70 percent of people. In the rest, T1 or another nearby level is as prominent or more so, and counting down from a level you have misread moves every level you then mark.
g.text: C7, the vertebra prominens
most prominent in only about 60 to 70 percent
of people, so counting from it can go wrong

g.data-tip: Level with the root of the scapular spine, the medial end where the spine of the scapula meets the vertebral border of the bone. Like every scapular landmark it travels with the shoulder, so the arm position has to be fixed before you use it.
g.text: T3 spinous process
level with the root of the scapular spine

g.data-tip: Level with the inferior angle of the scapula, but only with the person standing upright and the arms hanging at the sides. Prone, or with the arms raised, the scapula slides and the same angle commonly sits nearer T6. Record the position you examined in.
g.text: T7 spinous process
level with the inferior angle of the scapula
only when standing with arms at the sides

g.data-tip: The line joining the tops of the two iliac crests is used to find L4, both for lumbar puncture and for counting lumbar levels. In roughly 20 percent of people that line crosses L5 instead. This landmark has a known and quantified error rate, and it should be taught with it.
g.text: L4 spinous process
level with the tops of the iliac crests
at L5 instead in about 20 percent of people

g.data-tip: The posterior superior iliac spines show as a pair of skin dimples about 3 cm out from the midline, and they lie at the level of the S2 spinous tubercle. They are among the more reliably visible landmarks on the back.
g.text: S2, at the PSIS dimples
the dimples about 3 cm out from the midline
Three of these seven carry a published error rate. Learn the caveat with the landmark.
